title: SG-1.2 The Fundamentals of Six Sigma

1.2.1.examLens: Mostly recognition: what a process is, where it starts and stops, who the customers are, and which steps add value. The common question gives you a story and asks where the project scope should begin and end.

worked.question:
A team is asked to reduce late refunds. Customers complain that refunds take weeks. The refund request arrives by email, is logged, approved by a supervisor, and paid by finance. Which start and stop points fit best?
(A) Start: policy written. Stop: customer is satisfied.
(B) Start: refund request received. Stop: refund posted to the customer's account.
(C) Start: customer buys the product. Stop: product is returned.
(D) Start: supervisor approves. Stop: finance pays.
worked.solution: (B). It covers every step the customer experiences as "late." (A) is too vague and includes policy-writing. (C) covers the wrong process. (D) leaves out logging and approval delays, which are likely causes.

1.2.2.examLens: Turn a vague customer wish into a measurable requirement, and pick the best-written CTQ from a list.

worked.question:
A customer says, "I want my calls answered quickly." Which is the best CTQ?
(A) Answer calls promptly.
(B) 90% of calls answered within 30 seconds, measured from the end of the greeting to the first live agent.
(C) Reduce hold time.
(D) Agents should be polite and fast.
worked.solution: (B). It has a number (90%, 30 seconds), a unit (seconds), a limit, and an operational definition of when the clock starts and stops.

1.2.3.examLens: Classify a cost into the right category, and recognize that the same word (COPQ) is defined two ways.

worked.question: A plant reports: scrap $12,000; rework $9,000; warranty claims $30,000; complaint handling $6,000; incoming inspection $8,000; operator training $5,000. (a) Classify each. (b) What is COPQ under the ASQ-style definition? (c) What is the total under the PAF-style definition?
worked.solution:
(a) Scrap = internal failure; rework = internal failure; warranty = external failure; complaint handling = external failure; inspection = appraisal; training = prevention.
(b) ASQ-style COPQ = internal + external failure = (12,000 + 9,000) + (30,000 + 6,000) = $57,000. (Cost of good quality = 8,000 + 5,000 = $13,000.)
(c) PAF-style, all four categories = 57,000 + 13,000 = $70,000.

1.2.4.examLens: Read a Pareto chart, find the vital few, and notice when ranking by frequency gives a different answer than ranking by cost.

worked.question: Using the defect counts above, a scratch costs $2 to fix and a dent costs $15. Misalignment costs $10, paint runs $5, and other costs $4. Which category should the team attack first?
worked.solution:
Cost per category: Scratches 45 × 2 = $90. Dents 30 × 15 = $450. Misalignment 12 × 10 = $120. Paint runs 8 × 5 = $40. Other 5 × 4 = $20. Total = $720.
Dents cost the most ($450, about 63% of the total), even though scratches are more frequent. Re-ranking by cost: dents, misalignment, scratches.

1.2.5.examLens: This topic is calculation-heavy. None of these formulas is on the exam reference sheet, so know them. Watch for the difference between defects and defectives, and for rework hiding behind a high "final" yield.

worked.question:
A three-step process has FTYs of 0.95, 0.92, and 0.97. Separately, an audit finds 36 defects in 300 units, with 4 opportunities per unit.
(a) What is the RTY? (b) If 1,000 units start, how many are expected to pass all three steps first time? (c) What are the DPMO and the sigma level of the audit?
worked.solution:
(a) RTY = 0.95 × 0.92 × 0.97 = 0.874 × 0.97 = 0.848 (84.8%).
(b) 1,000 × 0.848 ≈ 848 units.
(c) DPO = 36 ÷ (300 × 4) = 36 ÷ 1,200 = 0.03, so DPMO = 30,000. Tail area 0.03 gives Z ≈ 1.88, so sigma level ≈ 1.88 + 1.5 = 3.38σ.

1.2.1.a.title: What a process is
1.2.1.a.html:
A process is a series of activities that transforms inputs into outputs. Everything you will do in DMAIC (mapping, measuring, improving) is applied to a process, not to a person or a department.
Example: order-to-cash takes a customer order (input) through entry, picking, shipping, and invoicing, and produces a paid invoice (output).

1.2.1.b.title: Boundaries and scope
1.2.1.b.html:
Every project needs a defined start point and stop point, stated as events, not vague phrases. List what is in scope and what is out of scope.
Example: "Starts when the customer submits a refund request. Ends when the refund is posted to the customer's account." Approving the company's refund policy is out of scope.
A boundary that is too wide ("end to end") makes a project impossible to finish. A boundary that is too narrow misses the cause.

1.2.1.c.title: Internal and external suppliers and customers
1.2.1.c.html:
• External customers are the people outside the company who buy or use the output.
  • Internal customers are the next step in the process. Each step is a supplier to the step after it.

Example: order entry supplies picking. Picking is order entry's internal customer, so bad data entered up front becomes rework later.

1.2.1.d.title: Value-added, necessary, and waste
1.2.1.d.html:
Every step falls into one of three classes.

  • Value-added (VA): the customer would pay for it, it changes the product or service in a way the customer cares about, and it is done right the first time.
  • Non-value-added but necessary (NNVA): the customer does not value it, but it is required by regulation, policy, or the current process design (for example required compliance checks).
  • Pure waste: neither valued nor required. Eliminate it.

Example: in a loan process, underwriting is VA. A legally required disclosure is NNVA. Re-keying the same data into a second system is waste.

1.2.1.e.title: Manufacturing versus transactional processes
1.2.1.e.html:
• Manufacturing processes make physical goods. Defects and delays are visible on the floor.
  • Transactional processes move information or deliver a service (invoicing, claims, hiring). Work-in-process is invisible: it sits in inboxes and queues. Waiting and handoffs are the main waste.

The same DMAIC tools apply to both.

1.2.1.f.title: Choose the start and stop points
1.2.1.f.html: Scope questions give a narrative and ask where the process should begin and end. Pick events that cover the problem described, nothing more.

1.2.2.a.title: What a CTQ is
1.2.2.a.html: A CTQ is a measurable characteristic of a product, service, or process that is critical to customer satisfaction. It comes from the voice of the customer, converted into something you can count or time.

1.2.2.b.title: The CTQ tree
1.2.2.b.html:
Work down three levels: Need, then Driver, then CTQ.
Example: Need = reliable lab results. Drivers = speed, accuracy. CTQs = "Results delivered within 4 hours for 95% of samples" and "Fewer than 2 reporting errors per 1,000 results."
Each CTQ ends in a spec: a number, a unit, and a limit.

1.2.2.c.title: Convert "fast delivery" into a measurable requirement
1.2.2.c.html: "Fast delivery" is a wish. A CTQ reads like: "Orders are delivered within 48 hours of being placed, for at least 98% of orders." Now everyone can measure it and agree on whether it was met.

1.2.2.d.title: The CTx family
1.2.2.d.html:
• CTQ: critical to quality
  • CTC: critical to cost
  • CTD: critical to delivery

All three are customer requirements expressed in measurable form.

1.2.2.e.title: Operational definition
1.2.2.e.html:
An operational definition says exactly how the characteristic is measured, so two people measuring get the same answer. It states what counts, where the clock starts and stops, in what units, and who measures.
Example: "Delivered" means the carrier scans the package at the customer's address, not when it leaves the warehouse. Without this, "48 hours" means different things to different people.

1.2.2.f.title: Choose the best-written CTQ
1.2.2.f.html: The correct answer has a number, a unit, and a limit. Words like "quick," "friendly," and "better" are wishes, not CTQs.

1.2.3.a.title: Internal failure costs
1.2.3.a.html: Defects found before the product reaches the customer. Scrap, rework, retesting, and downtime caused by quality problems.

1.2.3.b.title: External failure costs
1.2.3.b.html: Defects found by the customer. Warranty claims, returns, complaint handling, recalls, and lost sales. These are usually the most expensive because they also damage reputation.

1.2.3.c.title: Appraisal costs
1.2.3.c.html: The cost of checking quality: inspection, testing, and audits.

1.2.3.d.title: Prevention costs
1.2.3.d.html: The cost of stopping defects from happening: training, planning, FMEA, SPC, and mistake-proofing.

1.2.3.e.title: Two conventions
1.2.3.e.html:
The word "COPQ" is used two ways, and exam questions can follow either.

  • ASQ-style: cost of good quality = prevention + appraisal. COPQ = internal failure + external failure.
  • PAF-style (prevention, appraisal, failure; common in training material): all four categories are grouped together under COPQ.

Read the wording. If a question asks which costs are "failure costs," the answer is the same either way.

1.2.3.f.title: The hidden factory
1.2.3.f.html: Visible costs (scrap, warranty) are only the tip. Underneath are rework loops, extra inspection, expediting, lost customers, and wasted time. The "hidden factory" is the capacity a process spends doing work over again.

1.2.3.g.title: Classify the example
1.2.3.g.html:
• Rework = internal failure.
  • Inspection = appraisal.
  • Warranty repair = external failure.
  • Training = prevention.

A common trap is calling retesting after rework appraisal. It is an internal failure cost, because it exists only because the first pass failed.

1.2.3.h.title: Does COPQ include prevention and appraisal?
1.2.3.h.html: It depends on the source (see 1.2.3.e). If the answer choices force a decision and you cannot tell which convention applies, failure costs are the safest core of COPQ.

1.2.4.a.title: Vital few versus trivial many
1.2.4.a.html: Juran's insight: a small number of causes usually produce most of the problem. Roughly 80% of the effect comes from 20% of the causes. The 80:20 split is a rule of thumb, not an exact law.

1.2.4.b.title: Build a Pareto chart
1.2.4.b.html:
1. List the categories and count (or cost) each.
  2. Sort from largest to smallest.
  3. Compute each category's percent of the total, then the cumulative percent.
  4. Draw bars in sorted order with the cumulative line above them.

1.2.4.c.title: Read the chart
1.2.4.c.html:
Follow the cumulative line to roughly 80%. The categories to the left of that point are the vital few.
Example: defect counts are Scratches 45, Dents 30, Misalignment 12, Paint runs 8, Other 5 (total 100). Cumulative: 45%, 75%, 87%, 95%, 100%. Scratches and dents (75%) together, or the first three (87%), are the vital few.

1.2.4.d.title: Frequency versus cost or impact
1.2.4.d.html: Counting how often something happens is not the same as how much it hurts. A rare defect can be far more expensive. You can build a Pareto by frequency, cost, time lost, or customer impact, and the ranking can change.

1.2.4.e.title: Choosing focus, then re-running
1.2.4.e.html: Use the Pareto to decide where the project looks first. After improvement, re-run it: the old top bar shrinks and a new one may take its place.

1.2.4.f.title: The frequency leader is not always the target
1.2.4.f.html: If the question gives costs per defect, weight by cost and re-rank before choosing.

1.2.5.a.title: DPU
1.2.5.a.html:
DPU = defects ÷ units.
Example: 50 defects found in 200 units gives DPU = 0.25.

1.2.5.b.title: DPO
1.2.5.b.html:
DPO = defects ÷ (units × opportunities per unit).
Example: 50 defects, 200 units, 5 opportunities each. DPO = 50 ÷ 1,000 = 0.05.

1.2.5.d.title: Defect versus defective
1.2.5.d.html:
• A defect is a single nonconformance. One unit can have several.
  • A defective is a unit with one or more defects.

Example: 10 units contain 14 defects, and 8 of the units have at least one. DPU = 1.4, and the defective rate = 8 ÷ 10 = 80%. Do not mix them up in a formula.

1.2.5.e.title: First-time yield (FTY)
1.2.5.e.html:
FTY = units that pass a step the first time ÷ units entering the step. Units that are reworked or scrapped do not count as passing the first time.
Example: 100 units enter a step. 90 pass first time, 6 are reworked and then pass, 4 are scrapped. FTY = 90 ÷ 100 = 0.90. (Final yield = 96 ÷ 100 = 0.96, which hides the rework.)
When defects occur at random, FTY ≈ e^(−DPU). If DPU = 0.1, FTY ≈ e^(−0.1) = 0.905. This shortcut assumes a Poisson (random) pattern; the direct fraction is always valid.

1.2.5.f.title: Rolled throughput yield (RTY)
1.2.5.f.html:
RTY = FTY₁ × FTY₂ × ... × FTYₙ, the chance a unit passes every step first time. RTY is never higher than the lowest step FTY. It equals the lowest only if every other step is 100%.
Example: FTYs of 0.95, 0.90, and 0.98 give RTY = 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.98 = 0.838, or 83.8%. That is lower than 0.90.

1.2.5.g.title: Cycle time, lead time, takt time, throughput
1.2.5.g.html:
• Cycle time: time to complete one unit at a step.
  • Lead time: total time from order (or start) to delivery.
  • Takt time: the pace set by demand. Takt = available time ÷ customer demand.
  • Throughput: units completed per unit of time.

Example: an 8-hour shift has 480 minutes, minus a 30-minute break = 450 available minutes. Demand is 90 units. Takt = 450 ÷ 90 = 5 minutes per unit. A step with a cycle time above 5 minutes cannot keep up.

1.2.5.h.title: Process cycle efficiency (PCE)
1.2.5.h.html:
PCE = value-added time ÷ total lead time.
Example: 20 minutes of value-added work inside a 5-hour (300-minute) lead time. PCE = 20 ÷ 300 = 6.7%. Most of the time is waiting, not working.

1.2.5.i.title: Little's Law
1.2.5.i.html:
Lead time = WIP ÷ throughput rate.
Example: 60 orders in process, with 12 orders completed per day. Lead time = 60 ÷ 12 = 5 days. To cut lead time, reduce WIP or raise throughput.

1.2.5.j.title: Convert DPMO or yield to a sigma level
1.2.5.j.html:
Use the anchor table from 1.1.1, or the Z table for values between the anchors.

  1. DPMO ÷ 1,000,000 = tail area.
  2. Find that area in the Z table to get Z (long-term).
  3. Add 1.5 to report the sigma level.

Example: yield 98% means DPMO = 20,000. Area 0.02 gives Z ≈ 2.05. Sigma level ≈ 2.05 + 1.5 = 3.55σ.

1.2.5.k.title: Normalized yield
1.2.5.k.html: Extension. Normalized yield = RTY^(1/n): the average yield per step. For RTY = 0.838 over 3 steps, 0.838^(1/3) ≈ 0.943.

1.2.5.l.title: Hidden rework
1.2.5.l.html: A step can show 100% final yield because every bad unit is eventually fixed, while only 70% pass the first time. The correct input to RTY is first-time yield (0.70), not final yield. Questions that mention rework loops or "eventually all units pass" are pointing at this trap.

1.2.5.m.title: DPMO traps
1.2.5.m.html:
• Counting opportunities wrongly. Opportunities are defect chances per unit. They are not the number of units.
  • Mixing defects with defectives. DPMO counts defects. A defective rate counts units.
  • Forgetting the million. DPMO = DPO × 1,000,000.

1.2.5.n.title: Opportunity discipline
1.2.5.n.html: An opportunity must be a defined type or place where a defect can occur and be detected. If you redefine the opportunity count, DPMO changes without any real change in quality. Use the same count before and after, and agree on it up front.

1.2.1-1.stem: A SIPOC diagram's process column should list every detailed step of the process, including decisions and rework loops.
1.2.1-1.explanation: SIPOC is a high-level map with only 4 to 7 steps. Detailed steps, decisions, and rework loops belong in a detailed process map or swimlane map.

1.2.1-2.stem: A bank must send every customer a legally required disclosure before closing a loan. Customers do not value it, but it cannot be skipped. How should this step be classified?

options.html: Value-added, because the customer receives it

1.2.1-2.explanation: The customer would not pay for it, so it is not value-added, but the law requires it, so it is necessary non-value-added. Minimize it, but you cannot eliminate it today.

1.2.1-3.stem: A team is asked to reduce late invoice payments. The process: the sales order is confirmed, an invoice is generated, the invoice is emailed, the customer pays, and payment is posted. Which scope is best?

options.html: Start: the company writes its credit policy. Stop: the customer is happy.
Start: the invoice is generated. Stop: payment is posted.
Start: the sales order is confirmed. Stop: payment is posted.
Start: the customer pays. Stop: payment is posted.

1.2.1-3.explanation: Late payment can be caused by delays before the invoice is even generated, so the scope should begin when the order is confirmed. (A) is too vague. (B) misses early delays. (D) is too narrow.

1.2.2-1.stem: In a CTQ tree, which order moves from the broadest to the most specific level?
1.2.2-1.explanation: Start with the customer need, break it into drivers, then state each driver as a measurable CTQ with a spec.

1.2.2-2.stem: Two inspectors disagree about whether a package counts as "delivered within 48 hours." One counts from the moment the order is placed to the moment the package leaves the warehouse. The other counts to the moment the carrier scans it at the customer's address. What is missing?

options.html: An operational definition of "delivered" and when the clock starts and stops

1.2.2-2.explanation: An operational definition states exactly what counts and how it is measured, so two people get the same answer.

1.2.2-3.stem: Which TWO statements about a well-written CTQ are correct?

options.html: It is stated as the customer's wish in their own words.
It includes a number, a unit, and a limit.
It is set by the Black Belt without customer input.

1.2.2-3.explanation: A CTQ is a measurable characteristic with a spec. It is derived from the voice of the customer but is stated in measurable terms, not as a raw wish.

1.2.3-1.stem: After a batch fails final testing, operators repair the units and run the test a second time. The cost of the repair and the retest is best classified as:
1.2.3-1.explanation: The defect was found before the customer received it, so it is an internal failure cost. Retesting exists only because the first pass failed, so it is failure, not appraisal.

1.2.3-2.stem: A company pays for warranty repairs and spends staff time handling customer complaints. These are examples of:
1.2.3-2.explanation: The defects reached the customer, so these are external failure costs.

1.2.3-3.stem: Which TWO of the following are prevention costs?

options.html: An FMEA workshop before launching a new process

1.2.3-3.explanation: Prevention costs stop defects from happening (training, planning, FMEA, SPC). Final inspection is appraisal and scrap is internal failure.

1.2.4-1.stem: A Pareto analysis of defect counts shows: A 40, B 25, C 15, D 10, E 10 (total 100). Which categories make up roughly 80% of the defects?
1.2.4-1.explanation: The cumulative percentages are 40, 65, 80, 90, 100. The first three categories reach 80%.

1.2.4-2.stem: A team counts defect occurrences and the repair cost per occurrence: X occurs 50 times at $2 each, Y occurs 20 times at $20 each, Z occurs 30 times at $5 each. Which defect should the team attack first to reduce cost?

options.html: X, because it occurs most often
Y, because it costs the most in total
Z, because it is in the middle

1.2.4-2.explanation: Totals: X = $100, Y = $400, Z = $150. Y costs the most even though it is not the most frequent.

1.2.4-3.stem: The tallest bar on a Pareto chart is always the best target for an improvement project.
1.2.4-3.explanation: The tallest bar by frequency may not be the costliest or the most important to the customer. Weight by cost or impact before choosing.

1.2.5-1.stem: An audit of 500 invoices, each with 3 opportunities for error, finds 45 errors. What is the DPMO?

1.2.5-2.stem: A three-step process has first-time yields of 0.98, 0.95, and 0.90. What is the rolled throughput yield?
1.2.5-2.explanation: RTY = 0.98 × 0.95 × 0.90 = 0.838, or 83.8%. It must be below the lowest step yield (90%).

1.2.5-3.stem: A step reports a 99% yield because nearly every unit eventually passes, but 30% of units must be reworked before they pass. Which figure should be used as that step's yield in the rolled throughput yield calculation?
1.2.5-3.explanation: RTY uses first-time yield, which counts only units that pass without rework or scrap. The 99% figure hides the "hidden factory" of rework.

1.2.5-4.stem: A process has 90 orders in progress and completes 15 orders per day. What is the average lead time?
1.2.5-4.explanation: Little's Law: lead time = WIP ÷ throughput = 90 ÷ 15 = 6 days.

1.2.5-5.stem: An 8-hour shift has two 30-minute breaks. Customers demand 84 units per shift. What is the takt time?
1.2.5-5.explanation: Available time = 480 − 60 = 420 minutes. Takt = 420 ÷ 84 = 5 minutes per unit.

1.2.5-6.stem: A process step adds 12 minutes of value inside a total lead time of 4 hours. What is the process cycle efficiency?

1.2.5-7.stem: A process produces 66,807 defects per million opportunities. Using the 1.5σ shift convention, what is its sigma level?
1.2.5-7.explanation: 66,807 DPMO is the 3σ anchor. Check: area 0.0668 corresponds to Z = 1.5, and 1.5 + 1.5 = 3.0.

1.2.5-8.stem: Ten units are inspected. They contain 14 defects in total, and 8 of the units have at least one defect. Which statement is correct?

options.html: DPU = 1.4 and 80% of units are defective
DPU = 0.8 and 14% of units are defective
DPU = 1.4 and 14% of units are defective
DPU = 0.8 and 80% of units are defective

1.2.5-8.explanation: DPU = defects ÷ units = 14 ÷ 10 = 1.4. The defective rate counts units with one or more defects: 8 ÷ 10 = 80%. Defects and defectives are different counts.

1.2.4-1.text: Defect counts are: Chips 35, Misalignment 29, Burrs 28, Cracks 14, Stains 5. (a) Give the cumulative percentage for each category in order. (b) How many categories are needed to reach at least 80%?
1.2.4-1.answer: Total = 111. Cumulative: Chips 31.5%, Misalignment 57.7%, Burrs 82.9%, Cracks 95.5%, Stains 100.0%. (b) 3 categories (Chips, Misalignment, Burrs) reach 82.9%.

1.2.4-2.text: Defect counts are: Cracks 47, Burrs 44, Paint runs 40, Chips 14, Dents 5. (a) Give the cumulative percentage for each category in order. (b) How many categories are needed to reach at least 80%?
1.2.4-2.answer: Total = 150. Cumulative: Cracks 31.3%, Burrs 60.7%, Paint runs 87.3%, Chips 96.7%, Dents 100.0%. (b) 3 categories (Cracks, Burrs, Paint runs) reach 87.3%.

1.2.4-3.text: Defect counts are: Chips 57, Misalignment 41, Dents 17, Stains 9, Burrs 8. (a) Give the cumulative percentage for each category in order. (b) How many categories are needed to reach at least 80%?
1.2.4-3.answer: Total = 132. Cumulative: Chips 43.2%, Misalignment 74.2%, Dents 87.1%, Stains 93.9%, Burrs 100.0%. (b) 3 categories (Chips, Misalignment, Dents) reach 87.1%.

1.2.4-4.text: Defect counts are: Burrs 57, Chips 47, Paint runs 37, Scratches 19, Cracks 8. (a) Give the cumulative percentage for each category in order. (b) How many categories are needed to reach at least 80%?
1.2.4-4.answer: Total = 168. Cumulative: Burrs 33.9%, Chips 61.9%, Paint runs 83.9%, Scratches 95.2%, Cracks 100.0%. (b) 3 categories (Burrs, Chips, Paint runs) reach 83.9%.

1.2.4-5.text: A team compares defects by frequency and by cost. Dents: 64 occurrences at $20 each; Paint runs: 27 occurrences at $20 each; Stains: 79 occurrences at $5 each; Scratches: 50 occurrences at $35 each. (a) Which defect is most frequent? (b) Which has the highest total cost? (c) What share of total cost is it?
1.2.4-5.answer: Total costs: Dents $1,280, Paint runs $540, Stains $395, Scratches $1,750 (total $3,965). (a) Stains. (b) Scratches. (c) 44.1%.

1.2.4-6.text: A team compares defects by frequency and by cost. Scratches: 20 occurrences at $12 each; Cracks: 61 occurrences at $20 each; Dents: 63 occurrences at $12 each; Stains: 70 occurrences at $20 each. (a) Which defect is most frequent? (b) Which has the highest total cost? (c) What share of total cost is it?
1.2.4-6.answer: Total costs: Scratches $240, Cracks $1,220, Dents $756, Stains $1,400 (total $3,616). (a) Stains. (b) Stains. (c) 38.7%.

1.2.4-7.text: A team compares defects by frequency and by cost. Scratches: 34 occurrences at $35 each; Burrs: 43 occurrences at $12 each; Stains: 55 occurrences at $35 each; Chips: 56 occurrences at $8 each. (a) Which defect is most frequent? (b) Which has the highest total cost? (c) What share of total cost is it?
1.2.4-7.answer: Total costs: Scratches $1,190, Burrs $516, Stains $1,925, Chips $448 (total $4,079). (a) Chips. (b) Stains. (c) 47.2%.

1.2.4-8.text: A team compares defects by frequency and by cost. Dents: 56 occurrences at $5 each; Misalignment: 57 occurrences at $2 each; Chips: 75 occurrences at $12 each; Stains: 74 occurrences at $12 each. (a) Which defect is most frequent? (b) Which has the highest total cost? (c) What share of total cost is it?
1.2.4-8.answer: Total costs: Dents $280, Misalignment $114, Chips $900, Stains $888 (total $2,182). (a) Chips. (b) Chips. (c) 41.2%.

1.2.5-1.text: An audit of 200 units, each with 6 opportunities for a defect, finds 13 defects. Calculate DPU, DPO, and DPMO.

1.2.5-2.text: An audit of 300 units, each with 5 opportunities for a defect, finds 20 defects. Calculate DPU, DPO, and DPMO.

1.2.5-3.text: An audit of 500 units, each with 3 opportunities for a defect, finds 28 defects. Calculate DPU, DPO, and DPMO.

1.2.5-4.text: An audit of 800 units, each with 3 opportunities for a defect, finds 46 defects. Calculate DPU, DPO, and DPMO.

1.2.5-5.text: 100 units enter a step. 90 pass the first time, 4 are reworked and then pass, and 6 are scrapped. What are the first-time yield and the final yield?
1.2.5-5.answer: FTY = 90 ÷ 100 = 0.900. Final yield = (90 + 4) ÷ 100 = 0.940. The final yield hides 4 reworked units.

1.2.5-6.text: 200 units enter a step. 174 pass the first time, 16 are reworked and then pass, and 10 are scrapped. What are the first-time yield and the final yield?
1.2.5-6.answer: FTY = 174 ÷ 200 = 0.870. Final yield = (174 + 16) ÷ 200 = 0.950. The final yield hides 16 reworked units.

1.2.5-7.text: 400 units enter a step. 323 pass the first time, 44 are reworked and then pass, and 33 are scrapped. What are the first-time yield and the final yield?
1.2.5-7.answer: FTY = 323 ÷ 400 = 0.807. Final yield = (323 + 44) ÷ 400 = 0.917. The final yield hides 44 reworked units.

1.2.5-8.text: A process has 3 steps with first-time yields of 0.92, 0.93, 0.96. (a) What is the rolled throughput yield? (b) If 1,000 units start, about how many pass every step the first time?
1.2.5-8.answer: (a) RTY = 0.92 × 0.93 × 0.96 = 0.8214, or 82.1%. (b) 1,000 × 0.8214 ≈ 821 units. Note that RTY is below the lowest step yield (0.92).

1.2.5-9.text: A process has 3 steps with first-time yields of 0.99, 0.90, 0.98. (a) What is the rolled throughput yield? (b) If 1,000 units start, about how many pass every step the first time?
1.2.5-9.answer: (a) RTY = 0.99 × 0.90 × 0.98 = 0.8732, or 87.3%. (b) 1,000 × 0.8732 ≈ 873 units. Note that RTY is below the lowest step yield (0.90).

1.2.5-10.text: A process has 3 steps with first-time yields of 0.90, 0.96, 0.98. (a) What is the rolled throughput yield? (b) If 500 units start, about how many pass every step the first time?
1.2.5-10.answer: (a) RTY = 0.90 × 0.96 × 0.98 = 0.8467, or 84.7%. (b) 500 × 0.8467 ≈ 423 units. Note that RTY is below the lowest step yield (0.90).

1.2.5-11.text: A process has 4 steps with first-time yields of 0.98, 0.97, 0.90, 0.97. (a) What is the rolled throughput yield? (b) If 2,000 units start, about how many pass every step the first time?
1.2.5-11.answer: (a) RTY = 0.98 × 0.97 × 0.90 × 0.97 = 0.8299, or 83.0%. (b) 2,000 × 0.8299 ≈ 1,660 units. Note that RTY is below the lowest step yield (0.90).

1.2.5-18.text: A 420-minute shift includes 45 minutes of breaks. Customer demand is 120 units per shift. What is the takt time?
1.2.5-18.answer: Available time = 420 − 45 = 375 minutes. Takt = 375 ÷ 120 = 3.12 minutes per unit.

1.2.5-19.text: A 480-minute shift includes 30 minutes of breaks. Customer demand is 100 units per shift. What is the takt time?
1.2.5-19.answer: Available time = 480 − 30 = 450 minutes. Takt = 450 ÷ 100 = 4.50 minutes per unit.

1.2.5-20.text: A 420-minute shift includes 45 minutes of breaks. Customer demand is 90 units per shift. What is the takt time?
1.2.5-20.answer: Available time = 420 − 45 = 375 minutes. Takt = 375 ÷ 90 = 4.17 minutes per unit.

1.2.5-21.text: 50 units contain 62 defects, and 23 of the units have at least one defect. What are the DPU and the percent defective?
1.2.5-21.answer: DPU = 62 ÷ 50 = 1.24. Percent defective = 23 ÷ 50 = 46%. Defects and defectives are different counts.

1.2.5-22.text: 50 units contain 100 defects, and 29 of the units have at least one defect. What are the DPU and the percent defective?
1.2.5-22.answer: DPU = 100 ÷ 50 = 2.00. Percent defective = 29 ÷ 50 = 58%. Defects and defectives are different counts.
